images.title: 4.2 Site coverage and sample size per site
images.insight: Coverage is strongly uneven. The best-monitored sites log up to **363** readings across the year, while the sparsest — Kenyatta University, Nairobi, Thawabu, Mukuru CC — report fewer than **38** days each. These gaps are exactly the site-days a gap-filling model can reconstruct, but they also mean per-site statistics for the sparsest sites rest on very few days.

images.title: 4.3 Feature distributions
images.insight: PM2.5 is strongly right-skewed — most days sit in a low-to-moderate band around 20 µg/m³, with a long tail of high-pollution episodes up to ~136 µg/m³. Temperature and humidity are broadly symmetric. The skew motivates median-based imputation and warns that the *rare* high days carry most of the error.

images.title: 4.4 Correlation heatmap
images.insight: Within the basic sensor columns, temperature and humidity correlate only weakly with PM2.5 (r ≈ −0.09 and r ≈ 0.01) — weather alone explains little. The strongest signal sits in the *history* features built in §5 (rolling and lagged PM2.5, r ≈ 0.72/0.71).

images.title: 4.6 Weekday vs weekend
images.insight: Weekday and weekend PM2.5 distributions overlap heavily — the weekday effect is small (is_weekend correlates with PM2.5 at only r ≈ −0.04) but retained because it carries a little weekday traffic / activity signal and costs nothing.

images.title: 4.7 Which locations are most polluted
images.insight: Mean PM2.5 spans roughly 17 to 33 µg/m³ across the 74 sites. The most polluted are **Ol Leleshwa Road, UN Avenue Gigiri, Fire Station, Nairobi** — an east/north-east cluster consistent with industrial corridors; the cleanest are spread across green and lower-traffic areas. Location clearly matters, which §5.3 encodes as one-hot site columns.

images.title: 4.8 Temperature vs PM2.5
images.insight: Temperature is a weak negative driver (r ≈ −0.09) — warmer readings lean slightly lower, but the cloud is wide. Temperature carries far less information than what happened at the site in the last week.

images.title: 4.8 Humidity vs PM2.5
images.insight: Humidity shows essentially no linear relationship with PM2.5 (r ≈ 0.01). It is kept in the model anyway — it can still matter in non-linear splits and costs one column.

images.title: 4.9 Seasonal pattern: PM2.5 by month
images.insight: There is a clear annual cycle with a **Jun–Aug dry-season peak** and a lull around the long-rains months. Median and spread both grow in winter, so seasonality isn't just a shift in level — high days become both more likely and more extreme.

images.title: 5.5 Feature correlation with the target
images.insight: The engineered *history* features dominate: the 7-day rolling PM2.5 mean (r ≈ 0.72) and yesterday's PM2.5 (r ≈ 0.71) are by far the strongest associates of today's value. Among exogenous features the monthly cosine (r ≈ −0.38) captures the seasonal cycle. The 73 one-hot site columns are kept as a group — each is individually tiny but jointly they encode the genuine spatial variation of §4.7.

images.title: 7.2 Regression model comparison
images.insight: On the same held-out 20%, **XGBoost leads every metric** — RMSE 6.30 µg/m³, MAE 4.32 µg/m³, R² 0.66 — with Random Forest close behind (RMSE 6.46). The three linear baselines sit in a tight cluster around RMSE ≈ 6.7–6.8, confirming the boundary and history structure the trees exploit.

images.title: 8.1 Regression diagnostics — predicted vs actual, residuals
images.insight: Points hug the diagonal in the common band but spread as PM2.5 rises: **mean absolute error is ~3.3 µg/m³ on Good days, ~3.6 on Moderate days, and ~10.3 µg/m³ on Unhealthy days**, which the residuals panel shows is mostly *under*-prediction of real spikes. The model is well calibrated for typical days and systematically conservative on the rare extremes — the main limitation to communicate to users (§11).

images.title: 9.1 SHAP global importance (mean |impact|, bar)
images.insight: SHAP (TreeExplainer, exact for XGBoost) credits each feature with an exact µg/m³ amount. The last 7 days dominate (`pm2_5_roll7` ≈ 3.5 µg/m³ of mean |SHAP|), yesterday's reading next (`pm2_5_lag1` ≈ 2.7), then season (`month_cos`) and weather. Unlike split-based importance, SHAP assigns units — mean |SHAP| is the average µg/m³ each feature moves the prediction.

images.title: 9.2 SHAP local bars — clean, typical, and spike days
images.insight: On a clean day every bar points down and the prediction lands well below the 22.7 µg/m³ baseline. On the spike day (UN Avenue Gigiri, actual 118) *yesterday's PM2.5 alone contributes ≈ +52 µg/m³* — the model rides the persistent history's most recent value. That is the mechanism behind §8's under-prediction: when lag1 is missing, the model has no way to know a spike is underway.

texts.title: 3.1 Data dictionary & overview
texts.insight: 16,374 site-days × 11 columns (after dropping `pm10`), 74 sites, full year 2025. Constant columns (`frequency`, `network`, `site_id`, `device_name`) carry no signal and are dropped in §3.10.

texts.title: 3.5–3.6 Cleaning summary
texts.insight: Raw data hides faults as zeros: ~6.3% of temperature/humidity rows are zero (same probe) and 23 rows report PM2.5 = 0. Zero readings are treated as **missing**, then 596 target rows (3.6%) are dropped for an unusable `pm2_5`, leaving **15,778 modeled rows**.

texts.title: 3.7 Imputation policy
texts.insight: temperature and humidity are imputed with a **per-site median** (median survives the right-skew; per-site preserves each station's microclimate). For two sites whose weather probe never worked, a network-wide median fallback is used — their defaults are the least trustworthy in the demo.

texts.title: 4.1 Summary statistics
texts.insight: Mean PM2.5 ≈ 22.7 µg/m³, median ≈ 20.3 µg/m³, max 136.2 µg/m³ — a city whose typical day is 'Moderate' (US-EPA) but with real spikes. Mean temperature ≈ 22.2 °C, mean humidity ≈ 65%.

texts.title: 4.5 Outlier analysis — decision
texts.insight: IQR flags ~4% of rows including the high-PM2.5 episodes (up to 136 µg/m³). These are physically plausible pollution days, not sensor artifacts, so they are **kept**: removing them would teach the model to systematically under-predict the spikes this project cares most about.

texts.title: 7.1 Best model by RMSE
texts.insight: **XGBoost** wins on held-out RMSE (6.302 µg/m³ vs the next-best Random Forest at 6.460). The random split is same-seed for all models, so the comparison is fair.

texts.title: 8.2 Error by PM2.5 range
texts.insight: Errors are not uniform: Good (≤12) days have MAE ≈ 3.3 µg/m³ (n=245), Moderate days ≈ 3.6 (n=2,563), but Unhealthy (>35.4) days ≈ 10.3 with mean *signed* error ≈ −8.6 (n=348) — high days are systematically under-predicted. The model is most useful as a monitoring/gap-filling aid and least reliable exactly when a spike alert matters most.
